reflection.assumptions: The pandemic may have influenced patients’ ability to access services, trust health institutions, navigate disruptions in care, and interpret public health messaging in light of prior outbreak experiences. I recognize now that my perspective may have led me to overlook the nuances of community referral systems and the varied perceptions of healthcare effectiveness among different populations. I also see that my focus on barriers to care may lead me to miss the broader social and emotional contexts in which these barriers exist.
reflection.further_consideration: How do community referral systems impact individual access to healthcare during emergencies? Are there different levels of trust in healthcare systems among various demographics, and how does this affect their response to public health measures? Additionally, how do emotional responses to isolation and fear shape community behaviors during a pandemic?
reflection.reflexive_history:
1. [Phenomenon] Patient doubts effectiveness of healthcare system without traditional remedies
   [My code vs Peer code] My code: Patient doubts effectiveness of healthcare system without traditional remedies vs Peer code: Patient perceives traditional medicine as primary treatment
   [Evidence] 'People were having this concept that it won’t be treated by the English way unless I go for traditional native medicines that the only it could be treated.'
   [Interpretive difference] My code implies skepticism towards the healthcare system, while the peer code emphasizes the reliance on traditional medicine as a primary option.
   [Interpretive positioning] My emphasis on doubt reflects my concern about healthcare access; however, I can see how the peer's interpretation highlights the role of cultural beliefs in seeking treatment. I should be mindful of how cultural perspectives can drive patient choices and perceptions.
   [Next-round adjustment] I will consider how cultural perceptions of healthcare affect treatment decisions in future coding.

2. [Phenomenon] Government lockdown measures impacting daily life
   [My code vs Peer code] My code: Government lockdown measures impacting daily life vs Peer code: Government measures significantly impact daily life
   [Evidence] 'It one of the measures that government really put in place like the face mask and all of cause it affected people especially those with asthma diseases...'
   [Interpretive difference] My code focuses on the lockdown specifically, while the peer's code encompasses broader government measures.
   [Interpretive positioning] My lens emphasized the specific restrictions of lockdowns, potentially underplaying the overall impact of various government measures. This indicates a need to broaden my focus beyond just lockdowns to include other significant government actions.
   [Next-round adjustment] I will expand my focus in future coding to include broader government interventions and their cumulative effect on daily life.

3. [Phenomenon] Community self-restriction during pandemic
   [My code vs Peer code] My code: Community self-restriction during pandemic vs Peer code: Social isolation during lockdown
   [Evidence] 'we were not interacting, we were not visiting no one...'
   [Interpretive difference] My code highlights the voluntary nature of self-restriction, while the peer code addresses the social implications of isolation.
   [Interpretive positioning] My focus on self-restriction reflects a perspective of individual agency; the peer's interpretation highlights the emotional toll of isolation on community relationships. I realize I may need to integrate emotional aspects into my analysis of community behavior.
   [Next-round adjustment] I will incorporate more considerations of emotional and social impacts in future coding rounds.

coding_output:
Initial Code: Patient fear leads to decreased hospital visits  
Clues: "But as soon as they sound the bell that there is a confirmed case in Sierra Leone, the patients in-flow dropped drastically. ... The patients were scared. They were afraid."  
Initial Code: Increased responsibilities for health workers  
Clues: "It changed. It doubles up. ... Because I’ve to see the covid patients, and also do my normal clinical work."  
Initial Code: Implementation of triage process  
Clues: "But now it became compulsory as soon as you are at the hospital’s gate. ... But now it is instituted by management that all patients should have a triage form..."  
Initial Code: Emergency surgeries prioritized during the outbreak  
Clues: "We laid a law at the surgical department that only emergency patients will be operated on. ... All elective cases were put on hold."  
Initial Code: Initial panic reduced over time  
Clues: "But as time passes by, the effect of afraid became drain by people. ... They started doing their things, their normal activities."  
Initial Code: Shortage of PPE affects healthcare delivery  
Clues: "Because the way and manner in…..how the virus was being, and the lack of IPC gears at that point in time. ... There were few masks, few of the gowns to be used."  
Initial Code: Health facility management's response to COVID-19  
Clues: "the hospital management also called several meetings and also puts a lot of things and structures in place. ... encouraging people to wash their hands..."  
Initial Code: Overwhelming patient numbers from referrals  
Clues: "A lot of…. Two district- [retracted] district and [retracted] district have outbreak of covid in their theaters. ... So we were overwhelmed with patients at that phase."  
Initial Code: Mask-wearing becomes mandatory for healthcare workers  
Clues: "When I came here it was not….. people were bypassing the triage system. ... Now it became compulsory as soon as you are at the hospital’s gate."  
Initial Code: Patients reassured as time progresses  
Clues: "... people start to believe, to assume now that the corona virus is with us. ... There was no more panic."  
Initial Code: Changes in elective surgeries due to outbreak  
Clues: "Because at the height of the covid, everyone was afraid. So only emergency patients were operated open in the surgical department. All elective cases were put on hold."  
Initial Code: Training implemented for health workers  
Clues: "Yah. Trainings were held. That was a change. For example, for the use of the face masks, it was not compulsory in the hospital."  
Initial Code: Changes in patient treatment based on COVID-19  
Clues: "Those that were assigned to see covid patients, most of them were stopped from seeing none covid patients."  
Initial Code: Decreased patient flow during COVID-19  
Clues: "When the outbreak started, there were minimal patients that we saw at the department. Then there was this hold-up on elective cases, handling only emergencies."  
Initial Code: Increased staff training on COVID-19 care  
Clues: "Yes, there were trainings, especially in the line of covid-19. Were those staffs assigned to the covid-19 had their initial phase of training."  
Initial Code: Staff afraid of infection due to lack of protective gear  
Clues: "For me, I was afraid. I was scared. Especially when there is no glove, I don’t touch patients."  
Initial Code: General stress and fear among staff  
Clues: "Everyone was stressed. That was why many people were willing to attend the training. Because you were stressed of catching the virus."  
Initial Code: Dependence on government support for protective equipment  
Clues: "Later on the government then intervened and sent those IPCs- gloves, masks, the N95s."  
Initial Code: Communication about COVID-19 was sufficient  
Clues: "No, no. I don’t think so."  
Initial Code: Limited staffing due to COVID-19 training  
Clues: "Nurses that were trained on managing covid-19 patients, were withdrawn from seen none covid patients."  
Initial Code: Challenges in maintaining morale during training  
Clues: "The earlier phase of learning you will be enjoying it, but as time goes on you will be bored. You will be tired of the whole teaching."  
Initial Code: Importance of adequate IPC materials  
Clues: "There should be enough IPC material available for health care workers. Because, there is a saying: first, the know-how. You have to protect yourself first, before you take care of others."
